edition.sessionCovered: Mon, Nov 2 (oil drops on Iran-Qatar talks · Binance reopens withdrawals)
edition.stripNote: Mon 2 Nov. Oil −2% on Iran-Qatar talks — FM says Hormuz could reopen in 2 days. OPEC+ holds Dec quotas. Gold rebounds from 2026 low. Binance reopens withdrawals — 95% of $6.3B covered. BTC $78k. Midterms Tue. NFP Fri.
edition.scoreboardCaption: Mon 2 Nov vs Fri 30 Oct close. Grains reflect Fri 30 Oct. Ranked best to worst.
edition.commodleHint: Iran and Qatar entered a third straight day of diplomatic _____ to end the Hormuz war

overview: Oil fell on Monday as Iran-Qatar diplomatic talks entered a third consecutive day, with Iran's Foreign Minister Araghchi saying a Qatari-brokered plan could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington lifts its naval blockade and eases sanctions. Brent crude dropped 2.0% to $111.17 and WTI fell 2.3% to $101.71, pulling back from Friday's geopolitically driven rally. OPEC+ kept December production targets unchanged at a Sunday meeting; the bigger decision on 2027 quotas is expected at the full November 29 session. Gold rebounded 0.8% to $3,907 from Friday's 2026 low of $3,876, with silver bouncing 1.8% to $49.78 — both still down sharply on the month. Platinum and palladium posted small recoveries from last week's steep losses. Copper edged up to $6.52/lb on a weaker dollar.

Binance reopened crypto withdrawals on Sunday in phases, starting with Bitcoin, and said it has covered approximately 95% of the $6.3 billion stolen in Friday's hack from its SAFU fund and corporate treasury. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen, with the FBI confirming North Korea's involvement. Bitcoin recovered to approximately $78,000 (+1.6%) and Ethereum climbed to $2,290 (+3.2%), though US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643 million in net outflows on Friday. US midterm elections are tomorrow, with Democrats favoured to take the House; control of the Senate remains uncertain. President Trump said the Iran war would end 'very soon, one way or the other.' US nonfarm payrolls on Friday (consensus 65K) provide the next major macro signal, with the December rate-hike probability holding near 87%.

watchItems.title: US midterm elections — Tuesday, November 3
watchItems.text: Democrats are favoured to win the House (RealClearPolling average Dem 51.5% vs Rep 43.1%), while Senate control remains uncertain with key races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, and Iowa. The elections will shape Washington's approach to the Iran-Hormuz conflict: Trump has hinted at resuming strikes after the vote, while VP Vance's diplomatic track with Tehran continues. The midterms also carry implications for crypto regulation in the wake of the Binance hack — three crypto-backed PACs have spent approximately $170 million in the cycle.

watchItems.title: Iran-Qatar peace talks — potential Hormuz reopening
watchItems.text: Iranian and Qatari officials are in their third consecutive day of negotiations in Doha. Iran's FM Araghchi said a deal could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington lifts its naval blockade and eases sanctions. Iran's conditions include releasing frozen assets. A vessel was struck by a projectile in the strait on Saturday, and US Central Command has redirected 144 vessels. Trump said the war would end 'very soon, one way or the other.' Analysts warn that rhetoric could escalate after Tuesday's midterms, potentially pushing Brent toward $120.

watchItems.title: Binance recovery and crypto contagion watch
watchItems.text: Binance reopened withdrawals on Sunday, processing $4.65 billion in the first 9.5 hours against $1.01 billion in deposits — net outflows of $3.64 billion (2.1% of reported assets). The exchange says 95% of the $6.3 billion hack is covered and promises a full proof-of-reserves report on November 2. Ten assets are described as fully backed. The 95% figure and $6.34 billion set-aside are Binance's own claims, not yet audited. Strategy's Michael Saylor hinted at another Bitcoin purchase. Markets are watching whether outflows stabilise or accelerate.

watchItems.title: US nonfarm payrolls — Friday, November 6
watchItems.text: The October jobs report lands Friday at 8:30 AM ET with a consensus forecast of 65K. A weak print could ease the December rate-hike probability from its current 87%, providing relief to rate-sensitive metals and crypto. A strong number would reinforce the higher-for-longer narrative. The report is delayed three days from its usual first-Friday schedule. September's data showed a rising unemployment rate at 4.2%, and the labour market remains a key input for the Fed's December 8–9 decision.

desk.name: Gold
desk.sum: Gold rebounded 0.8% to $3,907 on Monday, finding modest support after Friday's 2026 low at $3,876 — roughly 30% below January's record near $5,608. Iran-Qatar diplomatic talks provided some safe-haven demand ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections. The December rate-hike probability remains near 87%, with NFP due Friday. Standard Chartered's support at $3,886 held; JPMorgan still expects rates to peak before gold finds a solid floor.

desk.name: Silver
desk.sum: Silver bounced 1.8% to $49.78 on Monday, recovering from Friday's plunge below $50 to its lowest level since November 2025. The metal remains down approximately 17% in October, its worst monthly decline in over a year, as rising real yields and higher-for-longer rate expectations have crushed the entire precious metals complex. The gold-silver ratio narrowed slightly from 79.3.

desk.name: Oil
desk.sum: Brent fell 2.0% to $111.17 and WTI dropped 2.3% to $101.71 as Iran-Qatar peace talks advanced to a third consecutive day. Iran's FM Araghchi said a Qatari-brokered plan could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if Washington meets Tehran's conditions, including lifting the naval blockade and easing sanctions. OPEC+ kept December production targets unchanged on Sunday; the full group meets November 29 to decide 2027 quotas. Analysts warn that rhetoric could escalate after Tuesday's midterms, potentially pushing Brent toward $120.

desk.name: Copper
desk.sum: Copper edged up to $6.52 per pound on Monday, supported by a weaker dollar and tentative risk-on sentiment from the Iran diplomatic talks. LME base metals broadly rebounded after last week's sell-off. Chile's September copper output fell 15.1% year-on-year to 387,870 tonnes, supporting the tightness narrative, but macro uncertainty ahead of midterms and NFP caps gains.

desk.name: Coal
desk.sum: Newcastle coal held at $152.45, consolidating near its highest level since October 2024. European TTF natural gas at approximately $31/MBtu ($105/MWh equivalent) continues to support coal-switching economics in Asia and Europe. Indonesia's export restrictions and the Hormuz disruption to Qatari LNG flows keep the supply side tight. October marks coal's best monthly performance since August.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.sum: Platinum edged up to approximately $1,440 on Monday, posting a modest recovery after last week's punishing sell-off. The metal remains down about 17% in October and roughly 51% below its January record of $2,924. WPIC's 265,000-ounce surplus forecast for 2026 and the 87% December hike probability add further downward pressure.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.sum: Palladium ticked up to $988 on Monday, recovering slightly from Friday's close below $1,000. The metal is down about 23% in October, the worst performer on the desk in percentage terms. Platinum substitution in gasoline catalysts and growing EV market share continue to structurally weigh on demand. Aerospace and superalloy end-uses provide a floor.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.sum: Iran-Qatar peace talks entered a third consecutive day on Monday, with FM Araghchi saying a Qatari-brokered deal could reopen the strait within two days if Washington lifts its naval blockade and eases sanctions. A vessel was struck by a projectile in the strait on Saturday. US Central Command has redirected 144 vessels. Trump said the war would end 'very soon, one way or the other,' while Secretary Rubio said the US has what it needs if it chooses to resume strikes. The full OPEC+ group meets November 29 to plan around uncertainty over the pace of recovery through the strait.

desk.name: Corn
desk.sum: December corn settled at 447¾¢ on Friday, down 3½¢ on the session. Managed money still holds substantial short positions. The US corn harvest is nearing completion and strong dollar headwinds persist. NFP on Friday and the midterm elections dominate near-term macro attention.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.sum: December wheat closed at 603½¢ on Friday, its ninth straight weekly loss. Russia allowed grain ships to leave Azov ports for the first time since July, adding supply pressure, though South Korea bought about 50,000 tonnes of US wheat. Record managed-money short positions and adequate global supply continue to cap rallies. Winter wheat planting remains on schedule.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.sum: November soybeans settled at 1,222¼¢ on Friday, finding modest support from near-term Chinese buying interest. The US harvest continues to run ahead of the five-year average, pointing to a large crop. Brazilian production estimates remain robust.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.sum: Bitcoin recovered to approximately $78,000, up 1.6% from Friday's post-hack low, after Binance reopened withdrawals on Sunday in phases and said it has covered 95% of the $6.3 billion hack from its SAFU fund and corporate treasury. About $3 billion of the stolen assets has been frozen. The FBI confirmed North Korea's Lazarus Group was behind the breach. Ethereum climbed 3.2% to $2,290. US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $643 million in net outflows on Friday, but Strategy's Michael Saylor hinted at another Bitcoin purchase.

desk.name: LNG
desk.sum: Asian LNG spot (JKM) held in the high $31s to low $32s per MMBtu. European TTF natural gas rose to approximately $30.8/MBtu, equivalent to about €105/MWh. Henry Hub fell sharply to $2.60, widening the gap between US domestic and global spot markets to historic levels. Hormuz disruption continues to threaten Qatar's 106 million tonnes of annual LNG export capacity, with no large ships transiting since early September.

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated with CFR Southeast Asia around $1,100–1,250 per tonne. Middle East FOB prices hold near $765 (Kuwait KPC). Hormuz disruption continues squeezing sulfuric acid supply chains — the essential input for copper leaching, phosphate fertilizer, and oil refining. Chinese domestic sulfur has firmed to approximately 7,200 yuan per tonne.

desk.name: Potash
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds near $367 per tonne. BPC settled a new India contract at $383 per tonne CFR, approximately $35 above China's 2026 benchmark. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. Seasonal fertilizer demand in the Southern Hemisphere provides modest support.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) held at approximately 90,000 yuan per tonne, flat since late October after sharp post-holiday declines from the 105,000-yuan high. SMM expects low-level sideways consolidation in the short term, though a second bottom test is possible if demand stays weak. Supply remains structurally tight under China's Document No. 46 export controls.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.sum: Gallium surged to approximately $2,100 per kilogram outside China as of early 2026, up over 130% since early 2025, as the Middle East conflict compounded China's Document No. 46 export controls. Chinese domestic gallium trades near 1,740 yuan per kilogram. Beijing's export controls retain a presumption of denial for US end users, and the Busan truce's Document No. 72 suspension has not meaningfully restored exports. China produces about 98% of global gallium.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds near $5.02 per pound, slipping from $5.44 in 2024 as steel demand softens. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but the timing of large-scale adoption remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.sum: ICE cocoa eased to approximately $5,400 per tonne by late October, correcting further from the August high of $6,821. Rising Ivory Coast arrivals and ICE inventories at a 2.25-year high continue to cap rallies, while El Niño forecasts affecting West African producers into 2027 provide support. The 1977 high of $5,104 acts as a pivot level.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.sum: Cobalt traded near $34,620 per tonne, little changed. The DRC (70% of global mine supply) maintains export quotas of 96,600 tonnes per year through 2027 to support prices, but the EV battery chemistry shift from NMC to LFP continues to structurally reduce demand. Glencore expects DRC exports to normalise in line with 2026 quotas.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate spot continued to trade near ¥97,500 per tonne, with Guangzhou Futures Exchange contracts near ¥92,000. Prices have roughly halved from the mid-May peak above ¥200,000. The selloff accelerated after SMM restated Chinese stockpiles by adding 175,000 tonnes to inventory estimates, and mine restarts at Bald Hill and Finniss added supply. Goldman Sachs projects the global market flipping to a 444,000-tonne surplus by 2028.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades around $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), little changed. Southeast Asian supply remains tight with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia — producing 70% of global latex — still affected by fungal leaf blight (Pestalotiopsis). Auto-sector demand remains solid, supported by replacement-tyre cycles.
